A profile of Alexandr Wang, who sources say is “an operator”, had “all” of Zuckerberg's support during Meta's AI revamp, and is being touted as his successor  —  The 29-year-old in charge of the company'
items.content_snippet: The 29-year-old in charge of the company's Superintelligence Labs is being touted as a potential successor to Mark Zuckerberg
items.summary_en: Amid Meta's aggressive AI strategic overhaul, 29-year-old Alexandr Wang has secured total backing from Mark Zuckerberg and is hailed by insiders as a relentless 'operator', even sparking speculation as Zuckerberg's potential successor. This rapid ascent highlights the tech giant's willingness to bypass traditional executive hierarchies, entrusting core strategic direction to a young generation of pragmatic technical operators amid the fierce AI arms race.

items.title: 企业级安全智能厂商Reach完成超5000万美元B轮融资
items.title_en: Reach Security, which develops AI-powered exposure management tools for securing enterprise systems, raised a $50M+ Series B led by Top Tier Capital Partners (FinTech Global)
items.author: FinTech Global
items.article_content:
Reach Security has secured more than $50m in a Series B round led by Top Tier Capital Partners, while unveiling Reach Everywhere, a launch that pushes its security control intelligence into every environment where defensive decisions are made.

Alongside lead investor Top Tier Capital Partners, the round drew backing from Ballistic Ventures, In-Q-Tel, M12, Microsoft’s Venture Fund and existing investors. Reach plans to direct the capital towards product development, broader integration partnerships, expansion overseas and further growth across US enterprise and federal markets.

The raise follows a year in which the firm’s customer count doubled, with Autodesk, Insurity, MPS and Ensemble Health Partners among the businesses using its technology.

The investment lands as attackers gain ground. VulnCheck’s State of Exploitation 1H-2026 report showed that under 1.3% of vulnerabilities are actually exploited in the wild, meaning the real challenge lies in reaction time rather than discovery.

CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report recorded an 89% jump in AI-enabled adversary activity, with breakout times falling to as little as 27 seconds, and AI is now linking exploits into previously unseen attack paths.

Reach responds by helping operations teams concentrate only on exposures and misconfigurations that remain genuinely reachable, ignoring those already neutralised by existing tools. Its AI independently reviews and adjusts each control, allowing defences to absorb growing attack volumes without extra staff.

When an adversary, or an AI agent a customer has deployed against its own estate, finds a way in, Reach shuts that route by reconfiguring security products the organisation already owns.

Reach Everywhere carries these insights into exposure management programmes, security operations centres, incident response processes, compliance platforms and frontier AI security environments, using the Reach API, its MCP server and a widening network of technology partners. Teams can therefore reprioritise backlogs and adjust controls inside the tools they already use.

A key early use case supports exposure management teams struggling with vulnerabilities that cannot be patched at the pace AI uncovers them. Reach locates, verifies and continuously tracks compensating controls, confirming they are active, up to date, enforcing policy and positioned in the correct attack path.

Where a change is safe, it routes the fix through ServiceNow, Jira or its own staged automation, testing it in a controlled environment first. An independent ROI study by TAG Infosphere found customers saved over 160 hours each week across control review, posture assessment and incident investigation, alongside a 156% return.

Reach describes itself as the trusted source of truth for enterprise security controls. Its deterministic AI continuously finds, analyses, validates and optimises controls, helping organisations map attack paths, cut risk and demonstrate that protections perform as expected. Through its API and AI-powered MCP server, AI systems can draw on live, validated control health data in place of stale inventories, exports or assumptions.

Reach Security CEO and co-founder Garrett Hamilton said, “What is old is new again in security. AI has given attackers better economics and a lower barrier to entry, but it has also given defenders a chance to use their home field advantage more than ever. Defending at enterprise scale requires an accurate understanding of what your defenses are actually doing. You can’t afford to get that wrong.

“That’s why a source of truth for your security controls matters so much: which ones are reducing exposure, which ones are falling short, and which ones can do more. That clarity is valuable to customers and to our joint integration partners.”

Reach Security co-founder and CTO Colt Blackmore added, “A compensating control that cannot be verified is not a mitigation. It’s an assumption. At human scale, incorrect assumptions create inefficiency. At machine scale, they create risk.

“Whether decisions are made by analysts, automation platforms or AI agents, the underlying truth about security control health must remain consistent, accurate and continuously validated. Our vision is to provide a trusted source of truth for security controls that makes those systems reliable, effective and safe to operate.”

items.title: 企业流程自动化平台Duvo完成3200万美元A轮融资
items.title_en: Duvo, which develops tech to automate business processes across enterprise systems, including ERPs and legacy apps, raised a $32M Series A led by Balderton (Mike Butcher/Pathfounders)
items.author: Pathfounders
items.article_content:
Tomáš Čupr tried to introduce AI agents at his online grocery startup Rohlik (he’s moved to chair and it’s now heading to an IPO). He didn’t get very far. He discovered that much of the company's operational knowledge just wasn't documented anywhere.

"Companies don't really understand their processes," Čupr told me. "There's so many things that live in people's heads, and people function as a sort of ‘human API’.”

His new startup, Duvo has now raised a $32m Series A led by Balderton Capital, bringing its total funding to $48 million. His bet is that he can target both large enterprises and the management consultancies advising them with a brand new approach to AI.

Existing investors Index Ventures, Northzone and Credo Ventures also participated. The funding will support Duvo's expansion into the US, initially targeting retailers and consumer goods companies.

Founded in 2025 by former Rohlik Group entrepreneur Čupr and his former head of AI, Duvo has developed what it calls an "Enterprise Execution OS", designed to automate business processes across disparate enterprise systems, including ERPs, spreadsheets, supplier portals and legacy applications.

Duvo's approach to getting at this ‘human API’ is to use AI agents to interview employees, analyse how they work and build detailed process maps. It then deploys agents to execute those processes across existing software systems, using APIs where available and interacting with screens where necessary.

But the technology also places Duvo in an interesting position relative to the management consultancy industry.

Čupr told me that the ‘process-discovery’ work traditionally carried out by firms such as McKinsey and Deloitte can cost enterprises millions of dollars. And even months to figure out. Duvo claims it can compress that work into weeks, before, crucially, automating the resulting processes.

"For consultants, we are compressing that discovery time," he said. "The discovery that would usually take many months of these junior people asking junior people and drawing these process maps, we can compress that into a couple of weeks."

Once again, we must all weep for those former junior hires, right?

So yes, that threatens a labour-intensive part of the traditional consultancy business model. And now they have a way to deliver results faster.

"Long gone are the times where a large consulting firm would walk in with the old school approach, trying to charge for the same amount of work that they used to charge," Čupr said. "Even consultancies need to reinvent themselves, and this is what we're enabling now." Got that, Deloitte?

Rather than positioning Duvo purely as a competitor to consultants, Čupr sees them as a distribution channel and implementation partner. The company now has an alliance with Deloitte Central Europe, which combines its expertise with Duvo's process-mapping and automation platform. Appropriate, given Čupr is Czech.

"We don't see it as either or," Čupr said, arguing that consulting firms can improve results by bringing broader strategic expertise, while enterprises with strong internal teams can use Duvo directly.

Indeed, Čupr’s longer-term ambition is to make enterprise AI automation something companies can buy and deploy themselves. No more expensive teams of specialist engineers.

"There's so many things that live in people's heads, and people function as a sort of ‘human API’.”

Could that mean the end of the Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE)  movement?

"If the product is built well, it should be self-deployable in a way," Čupr told me, comparing the experience to buying conventional enterprise software. "I think there was maybe a brief period in human history where AI needed [large numbers of] people to be deployed. I think we're past that."

Duvo claims to have unlocked more than $100 million in value for retail-style clients including Morrisons, Holland & Barrett, Boden, Notino and Allegro.

At Notino, the European online beauty retailer, Duvo claims its platform reduced a supplier-bonus reconciliation process from 70 days to 15, cutting specialist labour from around 120 hours per cycle to fewer than 10.

The company is also betting that enterprises will increasingly demand control over where their AI models run. While Duvo uses Anthropic models, it also operates GPU infrastructure capable of running open-weight models privately.

Čupr said the distinction is particularly important in Europe, where companies are often more reluctant than their US counterparts to send sensitive business data to external AI providers.

The company has almost 60 employees, but Duvo is entering an increasingly crowded enterprise AI market where many companies are still struggling to move beyond pilot projects.

It already has several well-funded VC-backed competitors, but the closest are Orby AI, Skan AI, Mimica, Sola and Scribe.

Orby AI (US, $35m raised; NEA, Wing VC, WndrCo, Pear VC). It’s a particularly direct competitor as it’s designed to learn business workflows. Its $30 million Series A in June 2024 was co-led by NEA, Wing VC and WndrCo. Skan AI is another, given Duvo's thesis about the undocumented ‘human API’. It raised a $63m Series C in August this year (Cathay Innovation, Dell Technologies Capital, Citi Ventures and others). And that’s just a couple worth mentioning.

For its US push, Duvo has recruited former Databricks and Salesforce executive Michael Green to lead go-to-market operations and former Kmart president and Accenture managing director Spencer Insolia to head its US business. Former Aldi South Holdings CEO Christoph Schwaiger has joined as a senior European adviser.

The company is also betting that enterprises will increasingly demand control over where their AI models run. While Duvo uses Anthropic models, it also operates GPU infrastructure capable of running open-weight models privately.

Čupr said the distinction is particularly important in Europe, where companies are often more reluctant than their US counterparts to send sensitive business data to external AI providers.

The company has almost 60 employees, but Duvo is entering an increasingly crowded enterprise AI market where many companies are still struggling to move beyond pilot projects.

It already has several well-funded VC-backed competitors, but the closest are Orby AI, Skan AI, Mimica, Sola and Scribe.

Orby AI (US, $35m raised; NEA, Wing VC, WndrCo, Pear VC). It’s a particularly direct competitor as it’s designed to learn business workflows. Its $30 million Series A in June 2024 was co-led by NEA, Wing VC and WndrCo. Skan AI is another, given Duvo's thesis about the undocumented ‘human API’. It raised a $63m Series C in August this year (Cathay Innovation, Dell Technologies Capital, Citi Ventures and others). And that’s just a couple worth mentioning.

For its US push, Duvo has recruited former Databricks and Salesforce executive Michael Green to lead go-to-market operations and former Kmart president and Accenture managing director Spencer Insolia to head its US business. Former Aldi South Holdings CEO Christoph Schwaiger has joined as a senior European adviser.

                Scarlet raises $50M Series B to accelerate AI medical device certification
                                    
                        Led by Headline, the funding will support the London-based company's expansion into the US and Asia-Pacific as it tackles lengthy certification processes for AI-powered medical devices.

                        Scarlet, the certification body for AI and software medical devices, today announced a $50 million Series B led by Headline, with participation from new investor Notion Capital and existing investors Atomico, Creandum, Kindred Capital, and Entrepreneurs First. Nancy Xiao Mclaughlin, Partner at Headline, joins Scarlet’s board.AI medical devices are being developed faster than certification bodies can review them. A company can train an AI diagnostic model in weeks and then wait 12 to 18 months for an assessment by experts, with another six to eight months of unnecessary delay for approval of a minor update, slowing down healthcare innovation.Scarlet is a government-designated certification body. Among the roughly 52 such organisations designated under the EU Medical Device Regulation, it is, according to the company, the only one that specialises in software and AI, and was truly built to enable AI’s iterative development. Scarlet holds designations from the EU, the UK’s MHRA, and the US FDA, where it is recognised as a Third Party Review Organisation.James Dewar and Jamie Cox founded Scarlet in London in 2021 after building AI medical devices at Babylon Health. The company spent its first three years working with regulators to obtain designation before issuing any certificates.Customers upload technical documentation to Scarlet’s AI-enabled platform in any format. Qualified reviewers then assess the submission against relevant regulations and ultimately issue a certification decision, deciding whether the product can be released into the market or not.Customers are typically building devices that use cutting-edge AI such as LLMs and computer-vision models, and include consumer giants like Flo Health, who boast over 500 million downloads, US radiology behemoth DeepHealth, the UK’s NHS England, cancer-detection AI company Skin Analytics, and AI Scribes such as Heidi Health and Tandem, who both recently announced nine-figure Series B fundraises.Scarlet also certifies the way AI products are actually built. Customers pay a subscription that covers ongoing surveillance, annual audits, and product changes. Because every assessment is consistent and every finding is evidenced, regulators can see the reasoning behind any certification decision at any time.“Scarlet has built a Notified Body for the AI world. The ability to release more rapid and frequent upgrades to our medical device ensures that our patients always have access to world-class care. We want to release upgrades to our medical device twice a month. We can with Scarlet,” said Finn Stevenson, co-founder and CEO of Flok Health.“For every day that safe and effective medical technology is not available, someone’s life takes a different course. Scarlet exists to solve this problem,” said James Dewar, Scarlet’s Co-founder & CEO.

“We’re building AI-native certification to help our customers bring cutting-edge innovation to patients around the world.”

“Scarlet helps regulation work with and for, not against, innovation. James and Jamie experienced the legacy certification process firsthand and decided to become the AI-native market enabler, starting with certifying AI and software as medical devices,” said Nancy Xiao McLaughlin, Partner at Headline.

“Scarlet has superpowers that seem at odds: they are fast, consistent, thorough, and rigorous. The team is devoted to its customers and takes seriously its mission to get life-saving technology to people faster. We’re excited to lead the Series B and for everything ahead.”

The funding will support Scarlet’s expansion in the United States and Asia-Pacific, growing its roster of expert AI reviewers and engineers, and expanding its certification offerings.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 总部位于伦敦的医疗器械软件合规认证平台Scarlet完成5000万美元B轮融资，由Headline领投。本轮资金将主要用于支持其在美国与亚太地区的全球合规服务扩张。这起融资的背景是全球监管机构对AI医疗软件审批标准的全面收紧，导致医疗科技研发机构面临漫长且高昂的过审壁垒，亟需自动化平台加速过审全生命周期。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: London-based Scarlet raised a $50M Series B led by Headline to fuel its expansion across the US and Asia-Pacific markets. The startup develops automated certification and compliance infrastructure for AI and medical device software. The funding comes as global regulators dramatically raise validation hurdles for clinical software, making compliance a mission-critical bottleneck.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI搞医疗模型可能只需几个月，但等药监局盖章能把创业团队活活熬死。做模型的都在烧钱互卷，做合规‘办证中介’的平台反倒闷声拿了半亿美金——淘金热里最赚钱的永远是给淘金者办准入许可证的人。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Training a healthcare AI model takes months, but securing regulatory stamps can easily outlive a startup's runway. While medtech developers burn billions competing on algorithms, the automated 'licensing bureau' quietly bags $50 million—selling regulatory tollbooths is the ultimate gold rush play.

items.summary_en: Japanese NAND flash giant Kioxia has shed two-thirds of its market capitalization since peaking last June as Japan's most valuable listed firm. The dramatic decline is triggered by cyclical memory headwinds and aggressive capacity expansion from emergent Chinese competitors. Capital markets are growing increasingly skeptical of Kioxia's long-term margin resilience in an increasingly commoditized flash market.

items.summary_zh: 日本存储巨头铠侠市值较去年高点蒸发三分之二，中国存储竞争对手崛起带来严峻挑战

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 日本闪存芯片巨头铠侠（Kioxia）自去年6月登顶日本上市公司市值冠军以来，股价持续遭遇抛售，总市值已缩水近三分之二。这一暴跌主要受制于全球消费电子存储周期性疲软，以及中国本土存储芯片制造商技术成熟与产能扩张带来的巨大价格压迫。投资者对铠侠在高阶存储市场的利润率及长期市占率产生深度疑虑。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Japanese NAND flash giant Kioxia has shed two-thirds of its market capitalization since peaking last June as Japan's most valuable listed firm. The dramatic decline is triggered by cyclical memory headwinds and aggressive capacity expansion from emergent Chinese competitors. Capital markets are growing increasingly skeptical of Kioxia's long-term margin resilience in an increasingly commoditized flash market.

elements_en.who: NAND flash maker Kioxia and global competitors
elements_en.where: Tokyo stock market and global semiconductor memory supply chain
elements_en.what: Market capitalization plunged by two-thirds from its all-time high
elements_en.why: Volatile memory cycle compounded by fierce capacity expansion and pricing pressure from Chinese rivals

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 去年刚戴上‘日本市值第一’的皇冠，转眼底裤都被打穿了。在芯片制造业，资本市场从来不听情怀故事，中国厂商只要把良品率和产能拉起来，老牌巨头如果拿不出断层领先的技术，就只能在价格战里被慢慢耗光估值。
ai_analysis.insight_en: One minute you're crowned Japan's most valuable company, the next you're down 66% as Chinese competitors ramp up fab capacity. The semiconductor market has zero sentimentality—if you cannot maintain an insurmountable technological moat, commodity pricing will crush your premium overnight.

items.title: 环境感知智能初创Mistlabs获2600万美元融资
items.title_en: Mistlabs, which develops Ambi, an ambient AI app for iPhone, Apple Watch, and Mac that learns about users from conversations, raised a $26M pre-Series A (Duncan Riley/SiliconANGLE)
items.author: SiliconANGLE
items.article_content:
SHARE


	
	
		
			
				
					
						UPDATED 09:00 EDT / OCTOBER 12 2026

Ambient intelligence startup Mistlabs Ltd. today brought its Ambi artificial intelligence system out of beta test on Apple Inc. devices, backed by $26 million in new funding.

Ambi is designed to act without being asked. Chief Executive Peter Mo said most AI platforms are built to complete tasks, and Mistlabs wants to see what becomes possible once software can “understand, reason and act in real time.” Ambi’s actions can sometimes come “before the user even thinks to ask,” he said.

To do that, Ambi learns about a person from the conversations it hears on their iPhone, Apple Watch or Mac, and Mistlabs said the software’s read on how that person likes to work sharpens over time. None of it is locked to a single device. Whatever Ambi is in the middle of follows the user from the Mac to the phone or watch.

A user who sets up a Routine hands a recurring job to several agents at once, and those agents work from everything Ambi has picked up about that person. In one example the company gives, someone sits through a meeting about competitors while the agents fact-check what is being said as the discussion unfolds. Ambi may have compared the rival products and drafted a proposal on the user’s MacBook before anyone leaves the room. The agents keep at it once the meeting ends, flagging missing information or new developments as the project moves along.

Further out, Mistlabs wants Ambi agents to negotiate with each other. The capability is due in the coming months and would come into play when two people using the software sit in the same meeting. Each agent would draw on what it knows about its own user, and together they would work out where the two sides’ priorities overlap.

Likely sticking points would surface as well. From there the agents are meant to bargain toward a result both people can accept, all while the conversation is still going. Users set the permissions that govern what their agent can do.

The $26 million raised ahead of the launch will pay for a standalone wearable Mistlabs is building to give Ambi more context about its users and their surroundings. Mo said hardware will let the system extend to “entirely new device types” over time. Luminous Ventures and Huaqin Technology Co. Ltd. led the San Francisco company’s Pre-A round. Huaqin, based in Shanghai, designs and manufactures smart devices for other brands.

Ambi is available now on Macs and on Apple devices that support iOS 18, with audio storage switched off by default. Anyone interested in the wearable can join a waitlist, and Mistlabs said the device will follow later this year.

items.summary_en: Ambient intelligence startup Mistlabs launched its AI system Ambi out of beta across Apple devices and announced a $26M pre-Series A round. Ambi is engineered to operate proactively across iPhone, Watch, and Mac by listening to conversations and anticipating user needs in real time. The venture aims to shift software interaction from passive prompt-based querying to autonomous multi-agent background execution.

items.summary_zh: Mistlabs完成2600万美元融资，其环境智能软件可跨苹果设备主动预判用户需求

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 环境智能初创公司Mistlabs宣布结束内测并正式上线其AI系统Ambi，同时完成2600万美元Pre-A轮融资。该系统深度整合于iPhone、Apple Watch和Mac之间，旨在通过后台环境监听与上下文学习，在无需用户主动发出提示词的情况下实时预判并执行任务。这一产品设计的核心理念是打破‘问答式AI’的被动交互局限，使多智能体能够无缝协同并在会议或日常工作中主动进行事实核查与流程调度。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Ambient intelligence startup Mistlabs launched its AI system Ambi out of beta across Apple devices and announced a $26M pre-Series A round. Ambi is engineered to operate proactively across iPhone, Watch, and Mac by listening to conversations and anticipating user needs in real time. The venture aims to shift software interaction from passive prompt-based querying to autonomous multi-agent background execution.

elements_zh.who: 初创公司Mistlabs及其首席执行官Peter Mo
elements_zh.where: 苹果生态（iOS、watchOS、macOS）及个人AI助手领域

elements_zh.why: 改变传统大模型需等待Prompt输入的被动状态，探索‘在用户提问前先行动’的环境感知计算

elements_en.where: Apple ecosystem (iPhone, Watch, Mac) and personal AI assistant market
elements_en.what: Raised $26M pre-Series A and brought proactive ambient system Ambi out of beta
elements_en.why: Overcoming the bottleneck of prompt-driven software by executing real-time autonomous agent workflows

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 宣传语说‘在你开口前就替你把事办了’，翻译过来就是你的手机、手表和电脑准备全天候合法偷听你讲的每一句话。资本最爱这种‘未来科幻感’，但用户在会议室看着AI自动替自己抢答时，真不知道该先夸它聪明还是先找隐私开关。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Marketing pitches it as 'acting before you even think to ask,' which is tech-speak for letting your phone and watch eavesdrop on your entire life around the clock. Investors love the sci-fi gloss, but good luck convincing corporate employees that a software listening to confidential board meetings won't leak their secrets.

items.title: 人力云巨头Workday宣布收购身份管理厂商C1
items.title_en: Workday agrees to acquire C1.ai, formerly known as ConductorOne, which develops enterprise software to manage human and AI agent identities and has raised $111M (Malia Spencer/Portland Business Journal)
items.author: Portland Business Journal
items.original_content:
Malia Spencer / Portland Business Journal:
Workday agrees to acquire C1.ai, formerly known as ConductorOne, which develops enterprise software to manage human and AI agent identities and has raised $111M  —  Software company C1, whose headquarters has fluctuated b
items.content_snippet: Software company C1, whose headquarters has fluctuated between San Francisco and Portland, is being acquired by California-based Workday Inc. (Nasdaq: WDAY).
items.summary_en: Cloud enterprise giant Workday agreed to acquire C1.ai (formerly ConductorOne), an identity governance vendor that had raised $111M. C1 specializes in access management infrastructure covering both human employees and autonomous AI agents. The deal equips Workday with critical security rails to manage and audit permissions as digital agents proliferate across enterprise workflows.
items.title_zh: 人力云巨头Workday宣布收购身份管理厂商C1
items.summary_zh: Workday宣布收购融资1.11亿美元的C1.ai，全面布局人类员工与AI智能体统一身份治理

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 企业级云服务巨头Workday正式达成协议，收购身份与权限治理软件商C1.ai（原名ConductorOne）。被收购方此前已累计筹集1.11亿美元资金，专门研发跨系统的人类员工及AI虚拟代理（Agent）统一身份与访问控制技术。Workday此次出手，旨在抢占大模型时代‘非人类数字员工’大量涌入企业后带来的全新权限管理与合规审计咽喉要道。

elements_en.who: Workday and enterprise identity startup C1.ai
elements_en.where: Enterprise SaaS and AI agent identity governance market
elements_en.what: Agreed to acquire C1.ai, which had raised $111M in venture capital
elements_en.why: Proliferation of autonomous AI agents demands unified identity governance alongside human staff

ai_analysis.insight_en: HR software used to just track human payroll and PTO, but now every autonomous agent wandering around the intranet needs its own digital security badge. Workday buying C1 is enterprise IT admitting that AI agents are basically wild interns who need strict permission walls before they accidentally wipe the database.

items.title: 大模型创企自曝人机工时比达一比六且初级技术招聘暴跌
items.title_en: Anthropic report on how AI is changing employment at the startup: decline of entry-level technical hiring, productivity boom across departments, and more (Anthropic)
items.author: Anthropic
items.article_content:
ResearchPolicyCommitmentsLearnNewsTry ClaudeEconomicsHow employment is changing at AnthropicOct 16, 2026Read in PDFNathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.

This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.

We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgement relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.

Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.

Anthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth.1

What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”

By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.

The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.

At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts. Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.

One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”

Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”

Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.

Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.

What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research, code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as 6 months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.

But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note however that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.

We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.

Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.

Do these patterns go beyond coding, into a broader transformation of knowledge work? Anthropic sales representatives steadily adopted AI agents starting last September. Figure 4 shows that after sales representatives adopt agents, they close deals with more clients. Part of this pattern could be driven by representatives with more sales opportunities selecting into automation. But it could also reflect automation of logging and routine communication. One account executive explained that Claude automations handled email drafting and customer management software integrations, replacing around 20% of their prior work tasks. Another noted that similar automations freed them up to focus on face-to-face time, letting them talk to 30% more of their customers than was previously possible: “anytime you do anything a second time, you're kind of like, okay, how can I use Claude to make it so that I don't have to do it a third time?”

Beyond sales, an Anthropic lawyer built a series of Claude automations to scan risks and opportunities, triage legal questions and take first passes through public-facing copy for legal review. A recruiter used Claude to help with candidate sourcing, tracking applications and an analysis that would have taken “maybe a couple of weeks,” freeing him to redesign outdated interview questions and meet with more applicants.

All of this suggests that as AI capabilities improve, it impacts a wide range of jobs across Anthropic. Descriptively, we see junior employment slowing in jobs that use Claude for the most complex tasks (Figure 5).

Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.

These ratcheting productivity expectations are dramatized by the cadence of internal model releases. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems in interactive coding agent sessions. We measure this with an automated Claude grader rating deidentified sessions’ task demands based on depth, scope and number of systems implicated. The share of tasks above the 90th percentile of difficulty for the old model rises sharply by around 30% (from 10% to 13% of all tasks) and stays elevated in the weeks following model releases. The easy end of tasks given to agents changes little.

Spiraling agent productivity translates into output pitched across humans’ screens and attention. One engineer compared this to babysitting:

They're like, I need my juice box opened and it's an emergency that my juice box is opened. And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding. [...] When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.

In the April 2026 survey, an open-ended question about how AI has impacted day-to-day work, 27% described productivity gains from Claude tools and 20% described their role shifting from actually doing work to managing Claudes.

Amid this model-driven acceleration, human attention is a constant bottleneck. In interactive, multi-turn sessions, the vast majority of agents’ session time is not spent working at all, but spent waiting. We track idle time by subtracting each agent’s active working time from each interactive session’s total wall-clock time. Claude sessions amount to around 80% idly waiting for human input. As one engineer put it, people are “bottlenecking the agents.”

Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.

One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”

Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”

Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.

Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.

What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research, code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as 6 months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.

But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note however that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.

We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.

Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.

Do these patterns go beyond coding, into a broader transformation of knowledge work? Anthropic sales representatives steadily adopted AI agents starting last September. Figure 4 shows that after sales representatives adopt agents, they close deals with more clients. Part of this pattern could be driven by representatives with more sales opportunities selecting into automation. But it could also reflect automation of logging and routine communication. One account executive explained that Claude automations handled email drafting and customer management software integrations, replacing around 20% of their prior work tasks. Another noted that similar automations freed them up to focus on face-to-face time, letting them talk to 30% more of their customers than was previously possible: “anytime you do anything a second time, you're kind of like, okay, how can I use Claude to make it so that I don't have to do it a third time?”

Beyond sales, an Anthropic lawyer built a series of Claude automations to scan risks and opportunities, triage legal questions and take first passes through public-facing copy for legal review. A recruiter used Claude to help with candidate sourcing, tracking applications and an analysis that would have taken “maybe a couple of weeks,” freeing him to redesign outdated interview questions and meet with more applicants.

All of this suggests that as AI capabilities improve, it impacts a wide range of jobs across Anthropic. Descriptively, we see junior employment slowing in jobs that use Claude for the most complex tasks (Figure 5).

Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.

These ratcheting productivity expectations are dramatized by the cadence of internal model releases. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems in interactive coding agent sessions. We measure this with an automated Claude grader rating deidentified sessions’ task demands based on depth, scope and number of systems implicated. The share of tasks above the 90th percentile of difficulty for the old model rises sharply by around 30% (from 10% to 13% of all tasks) and stays elevated in the weeks following model releases. The easy end of tasks given to agents changes little.

Spiraling agent productivity translates into output pitched across humans’ screens and attention. One engineer compared this to babysitting:

They're like, I need my juice box opened and it's an emergency that my juice box is opened. And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding. [...] When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.

In the April 2026 survey, an open-ended question about how AI has impacted day-to-day work, 27% described productivity gains from Claude tools and 20% described their role shifting from actually doing work to managing Claudes.

Amid this model-driven acceleration, human attention is a constant bottleneck. In interactive, multi-turn sessions, the vast majority of agents’ session time is not spent working at all, but spent waiting. We track idle time by subtracting each agent’s active working time from each interactive session’s total wall-clock time. Claude sessions amount to around 80% idly waiting for human input. As one engineer put it, people are “bottlenecking the agents.”

How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? An
items.summary_en: AI startup Anthropic released an internal labor research report revealing how deep agent adoption is radically transforming its workforce. AI agents now outwork human staff by a 6-to-1 ratio across tasks like bug fixing, scheduling, and project engineering, fueling an enterprise-wide productivity boom while causing a sharp decline in entry-level technical hiring. The study provides an empirical preview of how frontier AI companies are reshaping organizational design and entry-level career ladders.

items.article_content_zh:
根据该前沿人工智能实验室发布的劳动力重构专项报告，随着自研大模型与自动化智能体深入企业骨髓，该组织内部已演变为高度人机协同的全新形态。大量智能体全天候驻留于内部通讯应用和日历系统中，能够自主识别错误、修复系统漏洞，甚至在极少人工干预的情况下协同攻克大型工程任务。统计表明，自动化智能体的实际运行工时已经达到人类员工工作时长的六倍以上。

在生产力全面跃升的表象之下，企业的人才招募策略正在经历深刻的结构性逆转。传统科技公司赖以培养后备力量的初级技术岗位招聘比例明显缩水，公司倾向于保留少量能够精准指挥和评估AI集群的资深架构师与复合型人才，使得传统应届生依靠做杂活积累经验的“学徒制”成长阶梯几近断裂。这份基于跨部门数据与一线员工访谈的实证研究，向外界直观揭示了当全自动化范式普及后，知识型劳动力市场必将面临的残酷洗牌与职业断层。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 人工智能创企披露了其最新发布的组织与劳动力结构研究报告，详细展现了自研智能体全面嵌入日常工作流后的真实冲击。数据显示，公司内部智能体工作时长与人类工时比已攀升至6比1，日常排会、代码修障及复杂工程项目均被自动化接管，各部门迎来生产力爆发的同时，初级技术岗位的招聘比例出现明显萎缩。该研究旨在以前沿践行者的内部一手数据，为全行业揭示自动化工作流对传统人力梯队结构的系统性重构。

The study provides an empirical preview of how frontier AI companies are reshaping organizational design and entry-level career ladders.

items.content_snippet: High borrowing costs complicate AI lab's goal of achieving investment-grade status — Anthropic is offering Blackstone …
items.summary_en: AI developer Anthropic is assembling a massive $60 billion debt financing package to purchase Google TPU compute clusters. To entice private equity giant Blackstone to commit $9 billion to the deal, Anthropic is offering yields exceeding 10%. Driven by an insatiable appetite for computational power in the generative AI race, these exorbitant borrowing costs severely complicate the company's ambitions to secure an investment-grade credit rating.

items.title: Anthropic员工与大众AI预期大比拼
items.title_en: Survey of Anthropic staffers and US adults: 39% of US adults vs. 91% of staffers expect AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, and more (Anthropic)
items.author: Anthropic
items.article_content:
ResearchPolicyCommitmentsLearnNewsTry ClaudeEconomicsThe AI expectations gapOct 16, 2026Read in PDFSzymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, Charles I. Jones, Anton Korinek, Peter McCrory

How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the possibility that future AI models may be able to build their own successors (recursive self-improvement) could further accelerate the rate of progress. How quickly this might materialize and to what extent is unclear. Forecasts vary widely and are fiercely debated.

What is the core source of disagreement about AI's future impact on the economy? Is it principally due to differences in beliefs about how quickly AI capabilities will improve? Or does it reflect disagreement about how quickly and in what form those capabilities translate to real-world adoption? Which views on the future path of AI are consistent with rapid economic growth?

This note presents new survey evidence on these questions. In August 2026, we surveyed two groups: a sample of US adults that was nationally representative and Anthropic staff.1 The questions covered, among other things, AI’s capabilities, how widely it will be used, how much time it saves, how autonomous it will be, and how difficult it will be for a displaced worker to find a job in a different occupation.2 Anthropic staff build and use frontier AI every day. The second survey therefore shows how people closest to the technology anticipate its future, both in capabilities and in broader economic impact.

We report the following main findings. First, the two groups largely agree about what AI can do today but disagree about the pace of future progress. Anthropic staff expect capabilities to advance faster, AI to be used more widely and with less human involvement, and the time it saves on a task to be much larger. For example, 91% of staff expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared to 39% of US adults.

Second, there are sharp differences concerning people's own jobs. On average, staff members expect AI to be able to do 75% of their current work by 2030, compared to 28% for US workers overall.

Third, the two groups seem to reason about the labor market in a similar way: people who expect AI to do more of their own work in the future forecast higher unemployment. And, at the same level of expected AI automation of their own work, both groups forecast about the same unemployment rate.

We first investigate expectations about AI capabilities. We asked when AI will be able to do each of eight tasks as well as a skilled professional, from writing routine emails to making a Nobel-level scientific discovery. Both groups rank tasks in nearly the same order of difficulty (Figure 1, panel A).

The groups disagree on the path of future AI progress. For example, around a quarter of US adults and Anthropic staff think that AI can design, conduct, and publish scientific studies today. But by next year, 9 in 10 staff expect this to be feasible for AI as compared to just 38% for the general public. By 2030, 39% of US adults expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery (panel C), compared with 91% of staff. What is perhaps the most striking difference, depending on the task, between 19 and 40% of US adults say AI will never be able to do a given task, compared with at most 2% of staff.

In part, differences in views reflect differences in frequency of AI use. Among those who use AI at work regularly (about a fifth of respondents), 56% expect AI to be able to do at least seven of the eight named tasks by 2030. This is substantially higher than among all US adults (41%) and among those who have never used an AI tool (28%), but still well short of the staff view (96%).

The impact of AI on the economy is not solely determined by raw capabilities. People and businesses need to actually use AI, which takes time and experimentation. Of the work tasks AI will be able to do, US adults expect that 42% will be done with AI by 2030. Anthropic staff expect noticeably faster diffusion over the next few years, with AI used for 65% of all tasks for which it could be used.

To understand what might hold back AI adoption at work, we asked US adults to choose up to three obstacles from a list of nine that they expect to be the biggest. The general public expects that people's preferences and rules, more than the technological constraints, may be what holds adoption back (Figure 2). “Customers preferring to deal with a person” was the obstacle selected most often, followed by “data privacy and security concerns,” “AI not being reliable enough,” and “laws, regulations or liability.”

Notably, US adults who use AI regularly at work rank data privacy and security concerns first (42% consider it among the top 3 obstacles, compared with 37% among the rest) and see customer preferences to deal with humans as slightly less important (37% vs 42%).

The impact of AI on the labor market will in part depend on whether AI completes complex tasks autonomously or in collaboration with a human. The former tends to displace human workers. Alternatively, when AI complements human capabilities, workers become more productive. To get a sense for anticipated automation versus augmentation in 2030 among Anthropic staff and the general public, we asked how AI and humans will work together on various tasks ranging from email drafting to legal contracting by 2030. At Anthropic, the vast majority of staff say that by 2030 AI will either complete tasks alone or with a worker evaluating the work (Figure 3). By contrast, 4 in 10 US adults instead expect that humans will do most of the work themselves or with some AI help.

How much AI raises output depends not only on which tasks it can do and how widely it is used, but also on how much faster and better it does them. A technology that is just good enough to replace workers—what Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) call a "so-so" technology—displaces work without much increase in GDP. By contrast, a technology that completes tasks at a small fraction of cost or in a fraction of time can meaningfully raise GDP.

To measure perceptions about the productivity lift from AI, we asked the general public and Anthropic staff how long a task for which AI is well suited takes with AI, compared with doing it without AI. A task done in half the time corresponds to a doubling of output per hour.3

Anthropic staff report much larger expected savings, with 85% saying that it takes half the time or less. Among US adults who use AI at work, the typical answer is half the time, and 29% say the task takes just as long or longer, while only 5% of staff say so. Among US adults, 26% of those who use AI at work say a task takes a quarter of the time or less, and 21% of those who do not use AI at work say the same. For staff, that share is 59% (Figure 4).

Staff may be describing what they experience at work. As discussed further in How Employment is Changing at Anthropic, Anthropic employees increased productivity on some dimensions after adopting agentic tools: the lines of code engineers added tripled in the month after adopting coding agents and sales representatives closed more deals with clients after adopting AI agents. Output per person also rose in other business functions, like legal and recruiting.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we find a large gap in perceptions between the general public and Anthropic staff when it comes to AI’s impact on their own jobs (Figure 5). On average, Anthropic staff members say AI will be able to do 75% of their current work hours by 2030. US workers (respondents who report having a job) put the share at 28% on average, and only 1 in 20 say that AI could do 80% or more of their work hours by 2030.

Across US workers, expectations vary by occupation: AI is expected to be able to do 25% of work hours among manual trades, production and transport workers and 33% for workers in computer, engineering and science occupations. For this latter group, those who use AI regularly expect only 40%, a belief that is closer to the average US worker than to the average Anthropic staff member (75%).

How much of their own work people expect AI to do goes a long way toward explaining what they expect for the labor market. We told respondents that the current unemployment rate was about 4.2% and asked them to forecast the rate in 2030. Figure 6 groups respondents by the share of their own hours they expect AI to be able to do by 2030, and shows each group's average unemployment rate forecast.

US workers who expect AI to be able to do less than half of their work forecast unemployment of 7 to 8%. Above half, the forecast increases with the share of AI-exposed work. Those who expect AI to do 80% or more of their work expect, on average, an unemployment rate of 12.2% in 2030, above its peak during the Great Financial Crisis. Across US workers, ten more percentage points of work affected is associated with 0.4 points more forecasted unemployment. General optimism about AI does not explain this. Holding their own work exposure fixed, the share of the eight tasks a worker expects AI to master is unrelated to the forecast.

Even though their own reported exposure is much higher, the same gradient appears among Anthropic staff, with forecasts closely mirroring those of the general population. Therefore, these two groups do not seem to hold different theories of how AI will simultaneously affect their own jobs and the broader labor market. They have different experiences of what AI capabilities are and, in turn, expectations.

Even though Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do most of their work, they also expect Anthropic to keep hiring. 95% of Anthropic staff expect headcount to grow over the next 12 months, the median staff member expects it to grow by 66%, and 27% expect it at least to double. These are the personal expectations of staff members in an internal poll and do not represent Anthropic's plans or its view of its headcount. Even so, they show that automating tasks and shedding jobs are different forecasts, at least at a frontier AI lab.

Anthropic staff, however, are slightly more pessimistic than US adults about how quickly workers displaced by AI can find new work. We asked how long it would take a person who loses their job to AI automation in 2030—and who needs to switch occupations—to find a new one.4 The median Anthropic staff member expects that a worker displaced by AI would take 12 months to find a role in a new occupation. This compares to the median US adult response in the range of 7-12 months.

In Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI we introduced a structured framework for assessing how different future paths for AI capabilities and diffusion might translate into differences in economic outcomes. The model allows us to translate each respondent’s answers across five dimensions — capabilities, diffusion, automation, productivity, and worker transition frictions — into model-implied economic outcomes.5 Across both our US adult and Anthropic staff samples, we identify every respondent who answered all questions related to the key model inputs (3,259 US adults and 1,093 staff). We then evaluate the economic scenario implied by those answers for each respondent, focusing below on implications for GDP growth in 2030.

The median US adult's answers imply GDP growth of 5.4% in 2030, according to the model. The median staff member's answers imply GDP growth accelerating to 17.1% by 2030. There is significant variation within each group, so the distributions overlap widely (Figure 7). Figure A1 in the appendix shows how much each belief contributes to this gap.

Figure 7 also shows the economic scenarios implied by inputs provided by site visitors to an interactive scenario explorer based on this economic model that was published at www.anthropic.com/institute/econ-scenarios on September 9, 2026.

The interactive explorer asked shorter form versions of the questions we fielded to US adults and Anthropic staff in August 2026. 23,075 visitors completed the survey in the first 48 hours after publication, connecting from more than 140 countries worldwide. These visitors chose to come to a page on Anthropic's website and to take the quiz, so they are likely to be more interested in AI than the general public. Indeed, their answers place them between those of US adults and Anthropic staff: the median visitor's answers imply 12.5% growth.

One reason staff are more optimistic about AI capabilities may be that they have greater visibility into the development process. The Anthropic Institute recently published a report on progress toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), a process where AI systems increasingly improve their own capabilities (Favaro and Clark, 2026).

items.summary_en: Addressing escalating market scrutiny over political overreach in the chip sector, Intel leadership publicly clarified that the Trump administration holds no policy or intention to leverage a minority equity stake to interfere with Intel's corporate strategy. The statement seeks to reassure anxious investors following widespread speculation that government subsidies might morph into de facto state control over the struggling chipmaker's operational autonomy.

elements_en.what: Denying that the Trump administration has any policy to use a minority stake to dictate Intel's corporate strategy

									Apple’s new App Store rules crack down on AI nudification and ‘bait-and-switch’ apps				
				
											
													
						Marcus Mendes | Oct 16 2026 - 3:17 pm PT																
							
																1 Comment							
						
									
			
		
		
			
				
					


	
	

Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details.

Over the past year alone, there has been no shortage of reports and controversies involving apps that skirt Apple’s App Review Guidelines and expose users, including minors, to harmful or inappropriate content.

In January, the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) identified dozens of AI-powered “nudify” apps on the App Store.

Also in July, a 9to5Mac investigation uncovered dozens of apps disguising gambling platforms as simple games and utilities to evade App Store review, many of which were available to children.

These apps behaved as advertised when accessed from outside Brazil, but revealed hidden betting platforms when opened from Brazilian IP addresses.

And then there was the Grok controversy, which saw Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used to generate nonconsensual sexualized images of women and minors, prompting lawmakers and advocacy groups to call on Apple to remove X and Grok from the App Store. Apple later confirmed that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed unless the company addressed the issue.

Today, Apple updated its App Review Guidelines in an attempt to address problems such as these.

Under Section 1.2, which covers user-generated content, the guidelines now read (changes in bold):

Apps that enable users to create, generate, upload, share, or otherwise contribute content present particular challenges, including intellectual property infringement, nonconsensual intimate imagery, and anonymous bullying.

Apple’s new terms add that “Developers who fail to implement appropriate safeguards or fail to remediate identified violations after notice may be considered in violation of the Developer Code of Conduct.”

In another particularly important change, Apple strengthened its rules against so-called ‘bait-and-switch’ apps, which “misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval,” as the company puts it.

Don’t include any hidden, dormant, or undocumented features in your app; your app’s functionality should be clear to end users and App Review. Attempting to hide undocumented features in your app binary, such as through code obfuscation or other methods, is grounds for removal of your app from the App Store and termination of your developer account.

While the prohibition on hidden functionality was already present in Section 2.3.1, Apple has now made the rule more explicit, specifically calling out code obfuscation and emphasizing that violations can lead to an app’s removal and the termination of the developer’s account.

Finally, under Section 5 (Legal), Apple also strengthened its language around apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children, explicitly stating that they “will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.”

To read Apple’s updated App Review Guidelines, follow this link.

items.title_zh: 苹果严打AI脱衣应用及偷渡隐藏功能行为
items.summary_zh: 苹果更新应用商店审核指南，明令封杀AI一键脱衣软件，并严惩审核通过后热更新偷渡违规功能的应用

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果公司正式更新了应用商店审核指南，明令禁止任何提供AI一键脱衣或生成非自愿色情内容的应用上架。同时，苹果进一步收紧对“阴阳包”等偷渡行为的惩罚机制，严打那些在通过官方审核后借助云端配置或热更新解锁脱衣等隐蔽功能的操作。此举旨在应对生成式AI被滥用于制造深度伪造色情泛滥的监管压力与伦理危机，彻底封堵部分开发者钻空子绕过应用安全审查的灰色通道。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple has officially updated its App Review Guidelines to strictly prohibit apps that offer AI 'nudify' capabilities or generate non-consensual sexually explicit content. The updated policy also cracks down heavily on apps deploying hidden, undocumented features post-review via remote triggers. This enforcement targets the escalating ethical and regulatory fallout of deepfake abuse while shutting down devious loopholes used to bypass strict App Store scrutiny.

elements_zh.who: 苹果公司（Apple）
elements_zh.where: 苹果开发者平台与全球应用生态规则体系
elements_zh.what: 修订App Store审核指南，全面禁止AI脱衣应用，严厉惩处审核后私自解锁隐藏违规特性的违规行为
elements_zh.why: 防范生成式AI滥用造成的深度伪造色情泛滥与伦理法律风险，杜绝开发者通过热更新和云端开关规避审核

elements_en.where: Apple Developer platform and global App Store ecosystem guidelines
elements_en.what: Updated App Review Guidelines to explicitly ban AI nudify apps and penalize apps that reveal undocumented features after review
elements_en.why: To counter non-consensual deepfake pornography abuse and close regulatory loopholes where developers hide malicious features during inspection

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 上有开发者靠‘白天是修图神器、半夜云控变脱衣脱轨’的阴阳界面疯狂收割，下有库克手起刀落直接修补规则打地鼠。只要能绕过审查大赚一笔黑产钱，灰产们总能发明出比iOS沙盒机制还精妙的隐匿手段，苹果筑起的围墙花园永远在与人类最原始的欲望搞攻防演练。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Developers mastered the art of camouflage—presenting clean photo editors by day and remotely toggling nudify tools by night. Cook finally swung the banhammer, but as long as there is quick cash in taboo tech, Apple's walled garden will forever play an endless game of whack-a-mole with human primal instincts.

items.title: Replit掌舵人炮轰Anthropic性价比转投OpenAI
items.title_en: CEO Amjad Masad says Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, citing cost and saying "ChatGPT is better now"; source: the partnership is still in place (TechCrunch)
items.author: TechCrunch
items.article_content:
Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Lucas Ropek
	

									
									
								
					
					
						2:22 PM PDT · October 16, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly.

Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back.

Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models.

items.title_en: Apple says demand for iPhone Duo has been "nothing short of extraordinary"; deliveries slipped to late January within hours of preorders opening (Michael Acton/Financial Times)
items.author: Financial Times
items.original_content:
Michael Acton / Financial Times:
Apple says demand for iPhone Duo has been “nothing short of extraordinary”; deliveries slipped to late January within hours of preorders opening  —  Deliveries of the $2,000 Duo slip to 2027 within hours of going on sal
items.content_snippet: Deliveries of the $2,000 Duo slip to 2027 within hours of going on sale — Apple on Friday said its foldable iPhone Duo had seen …
items.summary_en: Within hours of opening pre-orders for its brand-new dual-screen foldable device, Apple announced that market demand has been nothing short of extraordinary. The massive influx of early orders quickly pushed delivery dates back by several months into early next year. This supply crunch highlights both intense consumer curiosity for new Apple form factors and early manufacturing yield constraints.

items.summary_zh: 苹果全新折叠屏设备预售启动后数小时内发货时间迅速延后，官方盛赞市场反响远超预期

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果公司在开启全新形态双屏折叠设备预售数小时后，官方对外宣布市场反响达到非同寻常的火爆程度。由于大量早期尝鲜订单集中涌入，原本的首批交付日期迅速滑落至数月之后，部分订单甚至排至明年初。这一供不应求的现象既反映了高端用户对新形态苹果硬件的极度渴望，也凸显了该机型复杂的精密铰链与柔性屏幕在初期产能爬坡上的巨大压力。

items.title: Meta削减两千五百万政治游说预算应对立法阻力
items.title_en: Filings: Meta reduced its $65M midterms budget by $25M through refunds, primarily from a super PAC it launched in 2025 with $45M to fight state AI bills (Theodore Schleifer/New York Times)
items.author: New York Times
items.original_content:
Theodore Schleifer / New York Times:
Filings: Meta reduced its $65M midterms budget by $25M through refunds, primarily from a super PAC it launched in 2025 with $45M to fight state AI bills  —  The company outlined a $65 million budget last year when it embarked o
items.content_snippet: The company outlined a $65 million budget last year when it embarked on an effort to elect state politicians friendly to the A.I. industry.
items.summary_en: Official campaign finance disclosures reveal that Meta slashed roughly $25 million from its planned $65 million midterms budget, largely through refunds from a dedicated super PAC established to push back against state-level AI regulations. The scaling back suggests Meta is recalibrating its aggressive lobbying tactics amid mounting public scrutiny and changing legislative battlegrounds.
